{{Short description|American mathematician (1926–2026)}}
[[File:William Alvin Howard May 2004.jpg|thumb|Howard in 2004]]
'''William Alvin Howard''' (December 11, 1926 – March 13, 2026) was a Canadian-born American mathematician and [[proof theorist]] best known for his work demonstrating formal similarity between [[intuitionistic logic]] and the [[simply typed lambda calculus]] that has come to be known as the [[Curry–Howard correspondence]]. He was also active in the theory of [[ordinal analysis|proof-theoretic ordinals]]. 

==Life and career==
William Alvin Howard was born in [[Vancouver]], [[British Columbia]], Canada on December 11, 1926.<ref name="CT">{{cite news |title=William Alvin Howard |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/obituaries/william-alvin-howard-chicago-il/ |access-date=31 May 2026 |publisher=Chicago Tribune |date=31 May 2026}}</ref> He received an undergraduate degree from the [[University of British Columbia]] and later received a master’s degree from the [[University of Illinois Chicago|University of Illinois]].<ref name="CT"/>

Howard earned his [[Ph.D.]] at the [[University of Chicago]] in 1956 for his dissertation "k-fold recursion and well-ordering".<ref>{{cite web | url=https://catalog.lib.uchicago.edu/vufind/Record/4242603/Holdings#tabnav | title=Holdings: k-fold recursion and well-ordering | publisher=The University of Chicago Library Catalog | accessdate=2015-05-04}}</ref> He was a student of [[Saunders Mac Lane]].

The [[Howard ordinal]] (also known as the Bachmann–Howard ordinal) was named after him.

Howard was the first to carry out an ordinal analysis of the intuitionistic theory <math>\mathbf{ID}^i_1(\mathcal O)</math> of inductive definitions.<ref>M. Rathjen, "[https://www1.maths.leeds.ac.uk/~rathjen/Sepp-chiemsee.pdf Proof Theory: From arithmetic to set theory]". Accessed 22 February 2024.</ref><sup>p.27</sup>

He was elected to the 2018 class of [[fellow]]s of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>{{citation|url=http://ams.org/profession/ams-fellows/new-fellows|title=2018 Class of the Fellows of the AMS|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|accessdate=2017-11-03}}</ref>

Howard died in Chicago on March 13, 2026, at the age of 99.<ref name="CT"/>
